source.title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy

page_placements.theme: Feature families, containment and co-activation modules within a single SAE

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures decoder-aligned feature pairs’ activation-support geometry and audits whether their contexts suggest sibling concepts. This bears conceptually on V3, but it does not reproduce a dictionary-size splitting experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper does not compare features across increasing dictionary sizes to test whether a coarse feature is replaced by children. It does report support geometry and semantic-context audits of decoder-aligned pairs, which bear on V3. Dominance, DAME, and general SAE benchmark results are omitted because they do not measure the stated splitting pattern.
record.test_reason: The study never tracks features across dictionary sizes and never identifies any pair as split from a coarser feature. It measures decoder-aligned pairs (cosine ≥0.7) within single SAEs, classifies their firing-support shape and audits their contexts, all framed as 'feature sharding'. The authors say the support categories 'describe support shape only'. These pairs are a related construct, not split-feature families, so the findings go under fits_no_version rather than being read as a V3 test. Splitting, absorption and canonical units are only discussed or cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' main conclusion is that the most dominant SAE features are less monosemantic and more redundant, which motivates dominance-aware evaluation. They present feature sharding as distinct from absorption, with which it can coexist. They report that decoder-aligned pairs show several support shapes, and that partitioning is more common among low-cosine controls, so sharding also needs context-level evidence. The sibling-reading cases are offered as context support for sharding, not as evidence about feature splitting.
record.recipe_differences: The study benchmarks SAE interpretability and redundancy, then examines decoder-aligned pair support and contextual judgments; it does not train matched SAEs at increasing dictionary sizes to track splits.
record.method_sensitivity: Support-shape classification uses decoder-cosine threshold ≥ 0.7 and stated firing-support criteria. Context judgments use two passes by GPT-5.6 Sol; the target pool and control-matched subset give different rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Among within-SAE pairs with decoder cosine ≥0.7, support shapes were 21.5% partition-like, 15.3% nested-like, 29.9% duplicate-like and 33.3% partial overlap. Low-cosine controls were 80% partition-like.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decoder-aligned SAE feature pairs show varied firing-support geometry; nested support is a minority pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: A blinded two-pass LLM audit gave a stable sibling-subclass reading to 15.8% of decoder-aligned partition-screened pairs (13.3% in the matched subset), versus 3.3% of low-cosine controls. About half of each panel had insufficient evidence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some decoder-aligned, support-separated pairs encode sibling subclasses (e.g. they vs he/she) of a shared parent concept.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature sharding: in a Pythia-160M TopK-65k SAE, a pair with decoder cosine 0.74 and encoder cosine 0.21 fires on separated contexts (Jaccard 0.019). Adding either decoder direction raises the same target logit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs can shard one decoder write across context-gated features with different encoders.

fits_no_version.finding: Sharding-compatible pairs make up 2.6–3.8% of decoder-redundant pairs across L0 bins (Appendix J.8, Table 42). No row records this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharding-compatible decoder-redundant pairs occur at low and high L0.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
record.problems: No dictionary-size splitting experiment is reported. The support categories describe pair geometry rather than proving that pairs are split features; the context audit has a high insufficient-evidence fraction and is based on selected panels. The authors also note limited combinations in the larger-model extension and hyperparameter-transfer limitations for some SAE architectures.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the tested V3 evidence were left out. General DAME, dominance, reconstruction, sparsity, and redundancy benchmarks were not included because they do not measure the stated splitting or hierarchy pattern.

untested.parts: No comparison across dictionary sizes; no coarse feature is tracked into finer children.
Larger models (Qwen3, Gemma-2-9B) are evaluated only for the DAME Q1 deficit, not for splitting.
Nested split families and hierarchy-mirroring across sizes are not tested. Only within-SAE decoder-aligned pairs are audited.
Absorption is discussed and distinguished from sharding. Parent-latent failure is not measured, nor whether changing size or sparsity fixes it.
No cross-size decomposition and no count of novel latents.
Matryoshka is benchmarked for DAME, redundancy and dominance, not for whether it changes splitting. The sparsity–dominance link is not a splitting measure.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3 labels are withdrawn. Decoder-aligned pairs within one SAE are not shown to be split features, and the authors disclaim that the geometry identifies splitting or hierarchy. A researcher could still treat the sibling audit (15.8% vs 3.3% controls) as weak, indirect evidence that geometrically close features can mirror sibling concepts. The audit uses an LLM judge, and roughly half of the cards were insufficient.

versions.untested_parts: No increasing-dictionary-size comparison tracking a coarse feature and its proposed children.
Larger and public SAE releases are evaluated for other metrics, not for size-related splitting across large models or releases.

The study examines decoder-aligned pairs and contextual sibling readings, but does not establish that they are nested families produced by increasing SAE size or that they mirror a representation-wide concept hierarchy.

The paper discusses absorption and reports support-containment categories, but does not test whether a general parent fails to fire when a specific child takes over, or whether size/sparsity changes fix this.
No cross-size decomposition of larger latents into smaller latents or analysis of novel latents across dictionary sizes.

The paper studies sparsity-related dominance and compares SAE architectures, including Matryoshka, but does not measure whether the training objective produces splitting or whether Matryoshka changes splitting.

relation.reason: It cites feature splitting in related work and discusses sharding against absorption (Chanin et al.) as a related pattern, without testing splitting.

tranche.reason: The study never tracks features across dictionary sizes and never identifies a pair as split from a coarser feature. It classifies decoder-aligned pairs within single SAEs as 'feature sharding', which it defines as distinct from absorption. The support categories are stated to describe support shape only.

source_check.notes: All five rows match the text. Section 4.2 gives +0.556/+0.611 and 15/18 and 16/18 in the same order the features are introduced (41902, then 46571). The text does not say 'respectively', so the feature-to-value mapping in r6/r7 is inferred from that order. Low-cosine controls are partition-like more often (80.0%) than matched high-cosine pairs (21.6%).

statements.problem: None. All numbers match Table 45 (equal-weight means of within-SAE percentages, five SAE families) and the Section 4.2 / Appendix J.9 pair case (0.7405, 0.2066, Jaccard 0.019, +0.556/+0.611 mean logit changes). The 80% low-cosine figure is from the matched comparison, whose high-cosine side is 21.6%, not 21.5%. That nuance is omitted but nothing is wrong.
